subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If f(x) = sin⁻¹√((x − β)/(α − β)) and g(x) = tan⁻¹√((x − β)/(α − x)), show that f′(x) = g′(x), where β < x < α.

mark_split.label: Reduce g(x) to the same θ

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.206, chapter 9 DIFFERENTIATION, Long Answer question 8. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints a CHAPTER-level marks banner (8M + 4M + 2 × 2M = 16M) but no per-step allocation on any answer. The split follows the shape this bank uses for a Maths-1B Section C question. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. Paper position: Maths-1B Section C runs Q19 to Q21 at 8 marks each, answer any 2 of 3, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The mathematics was checked independently before writing: three parameter pairs were used, (α, β) = (5, 1), (3, −2) and (2, 0.5), and at three interior points of each interval both f′(x) and g′(x) were computed as central difference quotients and compared with 1/(2√((x − β)(α − x))). All eighteen comparisons agreed to eight decimal places — for example α = 5, β = 1, x = 2 gives 0.288675135 for f′, for g′ and for the closed form. The question asks only for f′ = g′; the common value is given as well because it is one extra line and it is what makes the equality checkable.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what you substitute for x, and what both functions turn into.

steps.label: Substitute x − β = (α − β)sin²θ
steps.margin_note: First two marks. The substitution is chosen so that x − β becomes a sine squared and α − x becomes the matching cosine squared. Write both lines — the second one is what step 3 needs.
lines: Given f(x) = Sin⁻¹√((x − β)/(α − β))  and  g(x) = Tan⁻¹√((x − β)/(α − x)),  with β < x < α.
β < x < α makes x − β > 0, α − x > 0 and α − β > 0, so both radicands are positive and both functions are defined. That is what the given condition is for.
Also 0 < (x − β)/(α − β) < 1.
Put x − β = (α − β)sin²θ,  so  sin²θ = (x − β)/(α − β)  and  θ = Sin⁻¹√((x − β)/(α − β)).
Then 0 < sin²θ < 1, and taking the principal value gives 0 < θ < π/2.
α − x = (α − β) − (x − β) = (α − β) − (α − β)sin²θ = (α − β)cos²θ

recall.must_convey: That x − β = (α − β)sin²θ is substituted, which makes α − x equal to (α − β)cos²θ.
accept: put x minus beta equal to alpha minus beta times sin squared theta
then alpha minus x becomes alpha minus beta times cos squared theta
the substitution makes both differences into squares
x minus beta ni sin square theta tho substitute cheyyali
use sin squared plus cos squared equals one on the two differences
theta lies between zero and pi by two

steps.why: The two functions look different only because one has α − β underneath and the other has α − x. This substitution turns the first into a sine squared and the second into a cosine squared, so both fractions become one trigonometric ratio and the difference between the functions disappears.
common_mistakes: Substituting x = sin²θ directly, which ignores β and does not simplify either fraction.
Working with θ outside (0, π/2), where sin θ or cos θ can be negative and the square roots then need modulus signs.
steps.memory_tip: One substitution has to serve both functions, so it is built from the three differences x − β, α − x and α − β. Their relation (x − β) + (α − x) = α − β is the reason sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 fits.

steps.label: Reduce f(x) to θ
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The examiner wants the reason sin θ is positive and the reason θ lies in the principal range, not only the final line f(x) = θ.
lines: (x − β)/(α − β) = sin²θ, so
f(x) = Sin⁻¹√(sin²θ) = Sin⁻¹|sin θ|
0 < θ < π/2, so sin θ > 0 and |sin θ| = sin θ:
f(x) = Sin⁻¹(sin θ)
θ lies in (0, π/2), which is inside [−π/2, π/2], the principal range of Sin⁻¹.
∴ f(x) = θ

recall.must_convey: That f(x) = Sin⁻¹(sin θ) = θ, because θ lies in the principal range of Sin⁻¹.
accept: the fraction inside f is sin squared theta so the root is sin theta
sin inverse of sin theta is theta here
theta is between zero and pi by two so it is in the principal range
f of x theta ki equal avuthundi
the square root and the square cancel because sin theta is positive
f reduces to theta

steps.why: √(sin²θ) is |sin θ| and not sin θ in general, so the sign has to be settled before the modulus is dropped. The range 0 < θ < π/2 settles it and also puts θ inside the principal range, which is what lets Sin⁻¹ and sin cancel exactly.
common_mistakes: Writing √(sin²θ) = sin θ without saying why sin θ is positive.
Cancelling Sin⁻¹ with sin when θ has not been shown to lie in [−π/2, π/2].
steps.memory_tip: A square root of a square is a modulus. Deal with the modulus first, and only then cancel the inverse function.

steps.label: Reduce g(x) to the same θ
steps.margin_note: Two marks. This is the step the question is really testing: the SAME θ comes out of a different-looking function. The factor (α − β) cancels between the top and the bottom.
lines: (x − β)/(α − x) = (α − β)sin²θ/((α − β)cos²θ) = sin²θ/cos²θ = tan²θ
g(x) = Tan⁻¹√(tan²θ) = Tan⁻¹|tan θ|
0 < θ < π/2, so tan θ > 0 and |tan θ| = tan θ:
g(x) = Tan⁻¹(tan θ)
θ lies in (0, π/2), which is inside (−π/2, π/2), the principal range of Tan⁻¹.
∴ g(x) = θ

recall.must_convey: That (x − β)/(α − x) = tan²θ, so g(x) = Tan⁻¹(tan θ) = θ, the same θ as in f.
accept: alpha minus beta cancels and the fraction becomes tan squared theta
tan inverse of tan theta is theta
g also reduces to the same theta as f
g kuda ade theta ki vasthundi
sin squared over cos squared is tan squared
both functions give the same angle

steps.why: Once α − x is written as (α − β)cos²θ, the common factor α − β cancels and only sin²θ/cos²θ is left. That is the whole reason a sine inverse and a tangent inverse of two different fractions turn out to be the same angle.
common_mistakes: Using α − β in place of α − x in the denominator of g, which is the other function and defeats the question.
Writing √(tan²θ) as tan θ with no word about the sign, the same slip as in the previous step.
steps.memory_tip: f carries the whole interval α − β underneath and g carries only the part above x. The substitution splits α − β into sin²θ and cos²θ parts, so f sees a sine and g sees a tangent.

steps.label: Equal functions have equal derivatives
steps.margin_note: One mark. This is the sentence the question asks for. Say that f and g agree at EVERY point of the open interval, not at one point — equality at a single point would prove nothing about derivatives.
lines: For every x with β < x < α, both f(x) and g(x) equal the same θ.
∴ f(x) = g(x) for all x in (β, α)
Two functions that are equal at every point of an interval have equal derivatives at every interior point of it.

recall.must_convey: That f(x) = g(x) throughout the interval, so their derivatives are equal there.
accept: both are equal to theta so the two functions are the same
equal functions on an interval have equal derivatives
f of x equals g of x for every x between beta and alpha
rendu functions okate kabatti derivatives kuda okate
since they agree everywhere their slopes agree
that proves f dash equals g dash

steps.why: The derivative is determined by the values of a function on an interval, so two functions that agree on the whole interval have the same derivative there. Reaching f = g first is shorter and safer than differentiating each function separately and then comparing two messy expressions.
common_mistakes: Checking f and g at one value of x and claiming the derivatives are equal from that alone.
Differentiating f and g separately and stopping when the two answers do not look alike, without simplifying both.
steps.memory_tip: Equal on an interval means equal derivatives. Equal at one point means nothing about derivatives, which is why the words for all x are part of the answer.

steps.label: Find the common derivative
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One extra line gives the shared value, and it is the honest check on everything above: the result is symmetric in x − β and α − x, exactly as the two forms of the question are.
lines: Differentiate sin²θ = (x − β)/(α − β) with respect to x, taking θ as a function of x:
2 sin θ cos θ · (dθ/dx) = 1/(α − β),  that is  (α − β) sin 2θ · (dθ/dx) = 1
(α − β) sin 2θ = 2(α − β) sin θ cos θ = 2·√((α − β)sin²θ)·√((α − β)cos²θ) = 2√(x − β)·√(α − x)
f(x) = g(x) = θ, so f′(x) = g′(x) = dθ/dx

recall.must_convey: That the common derivative is dθ/dx = 1/(2√((x − β)(α − x))).
accept: differentiate sin squared theta equals the fraction to get d theta by dx
the common derivative is one over two root x minus beta into alpha minus x
two sin theta cos theta is sin two theta
d theta by dx kanukkovali, adi common derivative
the answer is symmetric in the two differences
both derivatives equal one by two root of the product
heard_as: x minus beta into alpha minus x

steps.why: Differentiating the substitution itself is shorter than differentiating either inverse function directly, because sin²θ = (x − β)/(α − β) has no inverse function in it at all. Writing (α − β)sin 2θ back in terms of x is what turns the answer into a formula in x.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as 1/((α − β) sin 2θ), which is correct but is still written in θ and not in x.
Writing the denominator as 2√((x − β)(α − β)), by using the wrong one of the two differences.
steps.memory_tip: The final denominator holds the two differences that meet at x: the part below it, x − β, and the part above it, α − x. Their product sits under one root.
